1. Seller workspace

Who: Sales team — BDE, SBDE and Team Leads (TL).
Job: call merchants and sell them a plan. ### How it works 1. Seller searches a merchant by Cust ID or phone and sees every past call. 2. Seller calls and logs the outcome (L0 / L1 / L2), e.g. Payment done, Callback, Not connected, Not interested. 3. On Payment done the seller picks the plan sold; on Plan Upgraded the portal shows only the higher plans allowed. 4. Seller clicks Send to Onboarding so onboarding starts at once. ### Business rules - Every call is its own record. Nothing is merged or overwritten, so the full history is always there. - Callbacks: the seller books a date/time; it appears in their "my callbacks" list on that day. - Not connected → WhatsApp: if the merchant didn't pick up (voicemail, disconnected, not connected), a WhatsApp goes out automatically with a "Request a callback" button. - Add a lead: sellers can add someone not yet in the merchant list; if they already exist, the portal points to the existing record instead. ### Lead Gen (Facebook / Meta ad leads) - New ad-form leads arrive every 5 minutes and land in the seller's Lead Gen pane. - One lead per person: repeat submissions from the same phone within 24 hours count as one lead. - A new submission after 24 hours is a fresh lead tagged "Repeat submission" — high intent. - If a seller already called that person, the lead goes to the same seller (tagged "Already called"). - Otherwise leads are shared round robin among sellers switched on for Lead Gen. Switching someone off keeps their existing leads with them. ```mermaid flowchart TB L["New Meta lead"] --> D{"Same phone
in last 24h?"} D -->|yes| M["Merged into existing lead"] D -->|no| K{"Already called
by a seller?"} K -->|yes| SS["Same seller"] K -->|no| RR["Next seller in rotation"] SS --> CALL["Seller calls → logs outcome"] RR --> CALL CALL -->|Payment done| ONB["Send to Onboarding"] CALL -->|Not connected| WA["WhatsApp with callback button"] classDef a fill:#dbe7ff,stroke:#3b6fd8,color:#0b1f4d classDef b fill:#d7f5df,stroke:#2f9e57,color:#0d3b1e classDef c fill:#ffe6cc,stroke:#d9822b,color:#4a2600 class L,D,K a class M,SS,RR,CALL b class ONB,WA c ```

Under the hood

| Mechanism | How it works | Why this choice | | --- | --- | --- | | Append-only call log | Every call is a new row in `calls`. The L0/L1/L2 label text is copied onto the row when saved. | Renaming an option later never rewrites history; audits and incentives always see what was actually picked. | | Disposition tree in the database | Options live in `disposition_nodes` (parent → child), not in code. | Admins can add or rename outcomes without a release. | | Lead Gen: least-picked round robin | Each new lead goes to the seller picked the fewest times since the roster last changed; ties go to whoever waited longest, then by name. | Plain "next in line" breaks when people join, leave or a server restarts. Counting picks keeps it fair and a newcomer starts level, not behind. | | Sticky assignment | Before the rotation, the portal checks if a seller already called this phone / Cust ID since the lead arrived — if yes, it goes to them. | Continuity: the merchant talks to someone who already knows them. | | 24-hour dedupe window | Same phone within 24 h = same lead; after 24 h = new lead tagged "Repeat submission". | Meta repeats rows and people submit twice; we want one lead, but a return visit days later is a strong buying signal. | | Phone → Cust ID linking | Last 10 digits of the phone are matched to the merchant list; once linked, the lead's calls move onto the Cust ID. Re-checked after every nightly merchant sync. | A lead is often not yet a known merchant; we never store a phone as a Cust ID by mistake. | | 5-minute polling | A Google Apps Script pushes new sheet rows every 5 minutes (max 1000 per batch). | The lead sheet is the source; no extra infrastructure needed. | | WhatsApp outbox | A not-connected call first writes a queued row in `wa_messages`, then sends; status becomes sent / failed. | If the WhatsApp API is down, nothing is lost — queued messages are retried. |

Worked examples

1. Lead Gen rotation. Three sellers are switched on for Lead Gen. Since the roster last changed, Amit has been picked 5 times, Bina 5 times, Chetan 4 times. - Next lead → Chetan (fewest picks). Now all have 5. - Next lead → tie between all three → whoever got their last lead longest ago, say Amit. - Dev joins the roster today → counting restarts from today, so Dev starts level with everyone instead of being 15 leads "behind" and getting the next 15 in a row. 2. Duplicate and repeat leads. - Riya submits the ad form at 10:00 and again at 10:05 → one lead (same phone within 24 h). - Riya submits again the next day at 11:00 → a new lead tagged Repeat submission (she came back — high intent). - Bina had already called Riya yesterday → the new lead goes to Bina (tagged Already called), not the next person in rotation. 3. Lead becomes a merchant. Riya's lead has only a phone number. Bina logs two calls against the lead. That night the merchant list sync shows a merchant with Riya's phone → the lead gets her Cust ID and Bina's two calls move onto the merchant's history, numbered after any earlier calls. 4. Counting a sale. Merchant 5678 gets Payment done from Amit on 22 Sep and again from Chetan on 25 Sep (re-logged). From 21 Sep a merchant counts only on their first-ever Payment done → the sale is Amit's; Chetan's entry doesn't count again.

Why

Sellers spend their time talking, not typing or deciding whom to call. Fresh leads are called within minutes (while interest is high), a lead someone already called stays with that person, and missed calls are recovered by WhatsApp.

2. Onboarding workspace

Who: Onboarding team (onboarders + onboarding admins).
Job: take a merchant who just paid and get their first ad live. ### How a case is opened A case opens from whichever happens first: 1. The seller clicks Send to Onboarding. 2. The CleverTap payment arrives (real time, when a field salesperson collects payment). 3. The next morning's Sub Raw sheet sync sees the subscription. The others then leave the case alone — so no paid merchant is ever missed, and none is opened twice. ### Who gets the case - New cases are shared equally among onboarders on the roster with "New cases" on (the live team): each goes to whoever has been picked the fewest times. - Language cases — merchants in Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Puducherry or Lakshadweep, or anyone tagged Language Barrier — go to onboarders ticked "Language". - An admin can move a case by hand when someone is absent. ### 8:30 AM daily rebalance Every morning the portal looks for "no talk yet" cases (never called, or last call was Not connected, with no callback booked): - The live team's no-talk cases move to the backlog team (everyone else on Onboarding), so the live team stays free for fresh payments. - The backlog team's cases are evened out, up to 10 per person. People keep their own cases first; only the extra moves. - Language cases are rebalanced only among the Language onboarders. - Every move is written on the case. ### Working a case - Onboarder calls and logs progress (L0 / L1 / L2): not connected, creative not satisfactory, technical issue, Ads Live, top-up, not interested… - Sheet data shows on each case: plan, credits, expiry, stage. - Technical issues can be opened and resolved without changing the main outcome. - Cases from on-ground Merchant Lending sellers are highlighted in yellow. - 10-minute alert: if a just-paid merchant isn't called within 10 minutes of being assigned (9 AM–7 PM), admins get a pop-up. ### Ads Live is double-checked Once a case is marked Ads Live and is a day old, the portal checks the real ad data: - No ad actually ran (no delivery, or only failed ads with 0 impressions and 0 spend) → the case is reopened and goes back to the queue; it no longer counts for Ads Live or incentives. - A merchant who went live on their own is recorded as Ads Live externally. ```mermaid flowchart TB P1["Seller: Send to Onboarding"] --> CASE["Onboarding case
(first one wins)"] P2["CleverTap payment"] --> CASE P3["Next-day Sub Raw sync"] --> CASE CASE --> LANG{"Southern state or
Language Barrier?"} LANG -->|yes| LT["Language onboarder"] LANG -->|no| ROT["Next onboarder in rotation"] LT --> WORK["Calls → logs progress"] ROT --> WORK WORK -->|Ads Live| CHK{"Ad really ran?
(checked next day)"} CHK -->|yes| CSM["Moves to CSM"] CHK -->|no| REOPEN["Case reopened"] REOPEN --> WORK WORK -->|not reached by 8:30 next day| RB["Rebalanced to backlog team"] RB --> WORK classDef a fill:#dbe7ff,stroke:#3b6fd8,color:#0b1f4d classDef b fill:#d7f5df,stroke:#2f9e57,color:#0d3b1e classDef c fill:#ffe6cc,stroke:#d9822b,color:#4a2600 class P1,P2,P3 a class CASE,LANG,LT,ROT,WORK,CHK,RB b class CSM,REOPEN c ```

Under the hood

| Mechanism | How it works | Why this choice | | --- | --- | --- | | One case per merchant ("first one wins") | Handoff, CleverTap and Sub Raw all check for an existing case first; only the first creates it, the others only add missing details (e.g. employee code). | Three sources, zero duplicates, zero misses. | | Least-picked round robin | Same fair rotation as Lead Gen: fewest picks since the roster last gained someone, ties → longest since last pick. Counted on the first person picked (`rotation_agent_id`), so if an admin later moves a case, the rotation stays fair. | Equal share of new cases, even if admins reshuffle by hand. | | Least-loaded fallback | If no roster is set up, the case goes to the onboarder with the fewest open cases. | Never leaves a case unassigned. | | Rule-based language routing | State from the merchant's address (or PIN code starting 5 / 6) marks a southern case; it goes once to the Language onboarder with the fewest open cases. | Merchants are served in a language they're comfortable with, which raises conversion. | | Once-a-day job lock | The 8:30 rebalance first inserts a row (job + date) into `daily_jobs`; if the row already exists it stops. | Runs exactly once a day even with several servers running. | | Rebalance algorithm | Target = even share per person, capped at 10. Each person keeps their most recently touched cases; the excess (oldest-touched first) goes to whoever currently has the fewest. Every move is logged on the case. | Greedy least-loaded balancing: fair, predictable, and the oldest-waiting merchants get fresh attention first. | | Ads Live reconciliation | A day after Ads Live, the case is compared to the real ad delivery data (impressions, spend). No real delivery → reopened and removed from Ads Live counts. | Trust but verify: incentives and Ads Live rate reflect ads that really ran. | | 10-minute SLA alert | Computed when the admin screen loads: today's real-time cases with no call from the current owner 10+ min after assignment, 9 AM–7 PM only. Reassigning restarts the clock. | Paid merchants are hottest in the first minutes. | | Fingerprint polling | The screen asks for a tiny "version" every few seconds and reloads the full list only when it changes. | Near-real-time screen without heavy reloads or extra infrastructure. |

Worked examples

1. One merchant, start to finish. | Time | What happens | | --- | --- | | Mon 11:00 | Field salesperson collects a Gold payment. CleverTap tells the portal. | | Mon 11:00 | No case exists → case created, goes to Neha (fewest picks on the live team), with the salesperson's employee code. | | Mon 11:12 | Neha hasn't called yet → onboarding admin sees the 10-minute alert and nudges her. | | Mon 11:20 | Neha calls, logs "creative not satisfactory" with a callback for Tuesday. | | Tue 09:30 | Sub Raw sync sees the subscription → case already exists → only refreshes plan, credits and expiry. | | Tue 15:00 | Neha logs Ads Live. | | Wed 09:30 | Sync checks real delivery: impressions > 0 → Ads Live stands; counts for Neha's incentive. Merchant now appears in CSM. | 2. If the ad never really ran. Same story, but on Wednesday the ad data shows only a failed ad with 0 impressions and 0 spend → the case is reopened, the Ads Live is removed from counts and incentives (kept in history), and the failure reason is shown on the case. 3. 8:30 AM rebalance. Live team: Neha has 4 cases nobody has spoken to yet (from before today). Backlog team: Raj holds 8 such cases, Sita holds 2 (cases already in conversation are never touched). - Neha's 4 move to the backlog pool → 14 cases for 2 people → even share 7 each (cap 10). - Raj keeps his 7 most recently touched; his oldest-touched 1 goes back to the pool. - Sita (fewest) receives cases until both have 7. - If the backlog team were already at 10 each, the extra cases would simply stay where they are. 4. Language routing. A new case's address is in Chennai (Tamil Nadu, PIN 600xxx) → southern case → goes once to the Language onboarder with the fewest open cases. A Maharashtra merchant is never treated as southern. A case later tagged Language Barrier by any onboarder is moved to the Language team at the next 8:30 rebalance.

Why

The first days after payment decide whether a merchant stays. Fast pickup, fair sharing, language-matched agents and an honest Ads Live check mean more merchants actually see results — and onboarders are paid only for ads that really ran.

3. CSM workspace (Customer Success)

Who: Customer Success Managers + CSM admin.
Job: merchants whose ads have run — keep them paying: renew, top up, upgrade. ### Who is in it Only merchants whose ads have actually run. Data refreshes every morning at ~9:30 AM from the tracker sheet. A merchant whose onboarding case was reopened stays with onboarding until an ad is properly live. ### Queues (each merchant in exactly one) | Queue | Meaning | What the CSM does | | --- | --- | --- | | Ending | Plan active, ad running now | Pitch a top-up or next ad before it ends | | Ended | Plan active, no ad running | Get the next ad live / top-up | | Cancelled | Plan active but merchant cancelled | Understand why, try to save | | Lapsed | Plan cancelled or expired | Win back with a renewal | | Onb lost | Onboarding closed as NI / Refund | Context only | | Closed | CSM's last call was NI / Refund | Leave alone until something changes | ### Business rules - CSM logs outcomes: Renewed, Top-up (with amount), Plan upgraded, Another ad live, Creative updated, Not interested, Refund requested. - CSM admin shares merchants among CSMs with weights, moves them when someone leaves, and adds pitch notes ("what to pitch") for one or many merchants. - Daily WhatsApps at 12 PM, chosen by situation: renew, ad ended (free / top-up), ad ending tomorrow (free / top-up). While the merchant stays in that situation, a reminder goes every second day. ```mermaid flowchart TB SYNC["~9:30 AM sheet sync"] --> Q["Merchant placed in one queue"] Q --> WA["12 PM WhatsApp
+ reminder every 2nd day"] WA -->|taps call me back| RCB["CSM Req Call Back list"] Q --> CALL["CSM calls"] RCB --> CALL CALL -->|Renewed / Top-up / Upgrade| PAY["Revenue → incentive"] CALL -->|NI / Refund| CL["Closed queue"] classDef a fill:#dbe7ff,stroke:#3b6fd8,color:#0b1f4d classDef b fill:#d7f5df,stroke:#2f9e57,color:#0d3b1e classDef c fill:#ffe6cc,stroke:#d9822b,color:#4a2600 class SYNC,Q a class WA,RCB,CALL b class PAY,CL c ```

Under the hood

| Mechanism | How it works | Why this choice | | --- | --- | --- | | Snapshot runs | The ~9:30 AM sync uploads in steps: start → subscriptions (in batches) → ads (in batches) → finish with expected row counts. Only a run marked complete is shown. | A half-finished upload is never visible; the switch to new data is all-or-nothing. | | Priority rules for queues | Rules are checked in a fixed order (onb lost → cancelled → lapsed → ending → ended); the first match wins. NI/Refund by a CSM overrides to Closed. | Every merchant lands in exactly one queue — no double work. | | Weighted round robin | Each new merchant goes to the CSM with the lowest assigned ÷ weight. The CSM admin sets weights (e.g. senior CSM = 2). Existing assignments never move. | People have different capacity; weights let the admin give some CSMs a bigger share while staying fair. | | Claim-once WhatsApp run | The noon run "claims" the latest complete snapshot by stamping it; only the first trigger that succeeds sends. It runs in the background after responding. | No merchant gets the same message twice, even if two triggers fire together. | | Reminder schedule | First message the day a merchant enters a bucket, then T+1, T+3, T+5… while they stay; each reminder is sent at most once. | Steady nudges without spamming; a missed day catches up. | | Stuck-message re-send | Messages queued for 10+ minutes but not sent go out on the next trigger. | Self-healing if a run was cut off. |

Worked examples

1. Weighted allocation. CSM admin sets Asha's weight to 2 (senior) and Vikram's to 1. Asha holds 40 merchants, Vikram 25. - Asha's share = 40 ÷ 2 = 20; Vikram's = 25 ÷ 1 = 25 → next new merchant goes to Asha. - Over time Asha ends up with about twice Vikram's merchants. Nobody's existing merchants are moved. 2. A merchant moving through queues. - Plan active, ad running → Ending (pitch the next ad or a top-up). - Ad finishes, plan still active → next morning Ended. - Plan expires → Lapsed. - CSM calls and logs Renewed → renewal counted for the CSM. - If the CSM had logged Not interested → Closed, until the CSM logs something else. 3. Reminder timing. A merchant enters Ended on Monday → WhatsApp Monday after 12 PM, then reminders Tuesday (T+1), Thursday (T+3), Saturday (T+5)… as long as they stay in Ended. If the run is missed one day, the reminder goes the next day — never twice.

Why

A merchant who sees results renews. CSMs focus on the right merchants at the right moment (ad ending, ad ended, plan lapsed), and WhatsApp keeps the conversation going even when nobody can call.

4. Not Interested / Refund merchants

When onboarding closes a case as Not Interested or Refund requested, or a CSM ever marks a merchant that way: 1. All normal WhatsApps stop for them. 2. They are flagged in CleverTap (Picom_dnd) so marketing campaigns skip them. 3. They get a short win-back WhatsApp with a testimonial for their category (optical, spa/salon, or general) — on day 0, then T+1 and T+3, between 12 PM and 7 PM. 4. If their case is reopened, the flag is removed. Under the hood | Mechanism | How it works | Why this choice | | --- | --- | --- | | Desired-state sync (outbox) | Table `picom_dnd_pushes` holds, per merchant, the value CleverTap should have (`want` true/false) and whether it's been pushed (pending / sent / failed). Every 5 min the pending ones are sent in batches of 500, up to 10 retries, with the last error saved. | CleverTap outages never lose an update, and a merchant leaving the bucket is automatically flipped back to false. | | Feature flags | `picom_dnd_enroll` and `winback_wa_live` in `app_settings` switch these features on; win-back goes only to a test merchant until live. | Safe rollout: test first, switch on without a release. | | Throttling | Win-back: max 150 per 5-minute run, only 12 PM–7 PM; leftovers go next run/day. | Spreads load and keeps messages in sensible hours. | | Suppression check | Before any other WhatsApp is queued, the merchant is checked against the NI/Refund list. | One rule protects every message type. | | Keyword template choice | Sub-category containing optic/eye → optical; spa/salon/parlour/beautician → spa; else general. | Relevant testimonial = better chance of winning back. | Worked example. Monday 10 AM an onboarder closes merchant 9012 as Not interested. - Within ~5 minutes → Picom_dnd = true is pushed to CleverTap (if it fails, it's retried every 5 minutes, up to 10 times). - Monday after 12 PM → win-back message (merchant is a salon → spa/salon testimonial). Again Tuesday and Thursday. - No renewal or not-connected WhatsApps reach 9012 any more. - Friday the case is reopened and no CSM has marked 9012 NI → Picom_dnd = false is pushed; normal messages can resume. Why: respect merchants who said no, avoid complaints, and still give them one fair, relevant reason to come back.

5. Callbacks & WhatsApp — shared by all teams

- Every WhatsApp we send has a personal "Request a callback" button. - When the merchant taps it, they appear in that team's Req Call Back list. - The Voice AI onboarding assistant can also hand a merchant to a human ("connect me to a person") — they appear in the onboarder's list, tagged Voice AI. - As soon as the team logs a new call for that merchant, the request is cleared. Under the hood: every message gets a random token in its link. A tap records the click on that message row; "open request" = clicked and not yet resolved. Any new call logged by that team for that merchant marks it resolved. A second Voice AI handoff while one is open bumps the same request instead of adding another (dedupe). Worked example. A seller can't reach merchant 3456 at 2 PM → WhatsApp goes out. At 7 PM the merchant taps Request a callback → 3456 appears in the Seller Req Call Back list. Next morning a seller calls and logs the outcome → the request disappears from the list. If the merchant taps again a week later, a new request is raised. Why: merchants answer when it suits them; the callback list turns a missed call into a warm, wanted call.

6. Incentives

All rules are date-based: a new rule gets a start date and old rules are never edited, so days already paid never change. Sellers - A sale = a Payment done call. From 21 Sep 2026 a merchant counts only on their first-ever Payment done (no double counting). - Weekly revenue plan (from 1 Oct 2026, Mon–Sun): each revenue level reached adds its payout. - Daily plan incentive: reaching a number of sales of a plan in a day unlocks a payout, plus extra per sale beyond. An upgrade counts as a sale of the new plan. - Team Lead earns on their own revenue plus half of what each of their BDEs earns that week. Onboarders & CSMs (from 1 Sep 2026) - Ads Live cases on a daily ladder. - Top-ups, each priced on its own: below ₹1,000 → nothing; up to ₹5,000 → 5%; above ₹5,000 → 10% of the whole amount. - Renewals (from 1 Oct 2026) priced the same way on the plan price — before Ads Live they belong to the case owner, after Ads Live to whoever logged them. Who earns: decided by team membership on that date (set in Manage Access → Teams). Finance gets an Incentives tab with a downloadable payout workbook. Under the hood: effective dating everywhere — teams, seller roles, plans and incentive rules are stored as rows with a start date, and the rule "in force" on a day is the latest one on or before it. Payouts are recalculated from the call log on demand, so they can always be reproduced. An automated check (`test-incentives`) guards the math. Worked examples. | Situation | Result | | --- | --- | | Onboarder logs a top-up of ₹800 | ₹0 (below ₹1,000) | | Top-up of ₹3,000 | ₹150 (5%) | | Top-up of ₹6,000 | ₹600 (10% of the whole amount, not just the part above ₹5,000) | | Renewal of a Gold plan (₹4,999) logged after Ads Live | Priced like a ₹4,999 top-up → ₹250 to whoever logged it | | Team Lead's two BDEs earn ₹2,000 and ₹1,000 in a week | TL gets their own slab payout plus ₹1,500 (half of each) | | Seller was BDE until 14 Oct, SBDE from 15 Oct | Days up to 14 Oct paid as BDE, from 15 Oct as SBDE — even if the change was entered later | Why: pay is transparent, matches the logged work, and can't change after the fact.

7. Admin & access

- People: create logins, reset passwords, deactivate leavers. - Access: who can open Seller / Onboarding / CSM / Incentives. Every change is recorded. - Teams with dates: moving someone from Sales to Onboarding "from Monday" updates their access and incentives automatically on that day. - Seller roles (BDE / SBDE / TL) also have start dates, so incentives use the right role for each day. - Rotations: who gets new leads (Lead Gen), new cases (Onboarding), language cases, and CSM allocation share. Under the hood: team moves are stored with a future date and applied automatically when the date arrives (checked on normal requests, throttled per server). Joining a team opens its workspace; leaving closes it and removes the person from rotations. Every access change is written to an audit log. Why: one place to run the team, with history — no guessing who had access or which role on a past date.

8. Analytics

- Seller analytics: total attempts vs unique merchants, fresh vs repeat merchants, connect rate, sales. - Onboarding analytics: cases handled, Ads Live (by onboarder and externally), Ads Live rate. - CSM analytics: calls, renewals, top-ups per CSM; overall retention. - Export: all call outcomes as CSV for reporting.

Why this order

- Merchant sync at 2:30, before everything. Phones and names must be in place first. That's why the no-phone WhatsApp retry waits until 9:00 — a case CleverTap opened yesterday may have had no phone until the 2:30 sync. - Rebalance at 8:30, before the 9:30 syncs. It only moves cases created before today that nobody has spoken to, so it doesn't need 9:30 data. Running before the shift means nobody's list changes while they're working. Today's 9:30 cases go straight to the rotation; if still untouched, the next day's 8:30 rebalance picks them up. - Both 9:30 syncs after the ~8:55 Gmail import. Both read AdsRun Raw. Running earlier would check Ads Live against yesterday's ad data and could wrongly reopen cases. - CSM sync and Sub Raw sync have no order between them — and don't need one. The CSM screen combines onboarding cases when it loads, not at upload, so a case reopened by the Sub Raw sync drops out of CSM whichever finished first. CleverTap MID linking reads both sources, so it also works either way. - Ad conversions at 9:40, after the ad data, because conversions are matched to ads by Ads ID; both are combined when the screen loads, so a small overlap doesn't matter. - CSM WhatsApps at 12:00, not 9:30. Leaves ~2.5 hours for the CSM sync to finish (including late or re-run syncs) and sends at a sensible hour. The run only uses a snapshot it hasn't sent yet — if today's sync is late, it won't re-send yesterday's messages; it waits and sends when today's run completes. - Picom_dnd and win-back on every tick, because they react to outcomes logged during the day, not to the morning data.

Risks & gaps

| Risk | Effect | Handled? | | --- | --- | --- | | Gmail import late (after ~9:15) and a 9:30 sync runs first | Ads Live checked against stale data; CSM queues a day old | Partly — fixed by the next day's run. Nothing checks that the import has landed. | | CSM sync fails midway | No new snapshot | Yes — screens keep yesterday's complete data; noon WhatsApps wait | | Lead Gen sheet trigger stops | No rebalance, retry, win-back or Picom_dnd; CSM WhatsApps only when someone opens the CSM page | No — needs a real scheduler (e.g. EventBridge on AWS) | | Two 9:30 syncs run at once | Both write to the database together | Yes — different tables; "first one wins" for cases |
💡 Suggested fix: make both 9:30 syncs first check that today's AdsRun Raw import has landed (e.g. latest ad date or a "last imported" cell) and retry 15 minutes later if not. Closes the stale-ad-data gap.

10. What happens when something goes wrong

| If… | Then… | Recovery | | --- | --- | --- | | The 5-minute lead sheet sync stops | No new Lead Gen leads; 8:30 rebalance, win-back and CleverTap flag stop; CSM WhatsApps only go when someone opens the CSM page | Fix the sheet trigger; everything catches up on the next run | | The WhatsApp API is down | Messages stay queued in the database | Re-sent automatically on the next run (CSM ones after 10 minutes) | | CleverTap is down | Picom_dnd pushes are marked failed with the error | Retried every 5 minutes, up to 10 times | | A CleverTap payment webhook is missed | No instant case | The 9:30 Sub Raw sync opens the case next morning | | CleverTap sends only a MID | Payment stored as unmatched | Linked to the Cust ID at the next Sub Raw sync | | Nobody is switched on for Lead Gen | Leads wait unassigned | Assigned as soon as someone is switched on | | No Language onboarder is ticked | Southern cases stay with normal onboarders | Picked up once someone is ticked | | A CSM sync upload breaks midway | The run never becomes "complete" | Screens keep showing yesterday's complete data | | An onboarder leaves | Removed from rotations on their leaving date | Admin reassigns their open cases |

11. Mechanisms at a glance

ℹ️ There is no separate message broker (no SQS / Kafka / Redis). Every "queue" here is a Postgres table with a status column, and timing comes from the 5-minute sheet sync. Simple to run, easy to inspect — and worth keeping in mind for the AWS move.
| Mechanism | Used in | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Least-picked round robin | Lead Gen leads, new onboarding cases | Fair share that survives people joining/leaving and restarts | | Weighted round robin | CSM merchant allocation | Different capacity per CSM | | Least-loaded assignment | Language cases, 8:30 rebalance, no-roster fallback | Balance current workload, not just new work | | Sticky / affinity | Lead already called by a seller | Continuity with the same person | | Outbox queue (status table) | WhatsApp (`wa_messages`), CleverTap flag (`picom_dnd_pushes`) | Survive outages, retry, full trace | | Once-per-day lock | 8:30 rebalance (`daily_jobs`) | Exactly once, even on many servers | | Claim-once | CSM noon WhatsApp run | No duplicate messages | | Snapshot + "complete" flag | CSM ~9:30 AM sync | Never show half-uploaded data | | Dedupe windows | Lead Gen 24 h, Voice AI open request | Avoid repeats | | Append-only + label snapshot | Calls and onboarding/CSM events | Untouchable history | | Effective dating | Teams, roles, plans, incentives | Reproducible payouts | | Reconciliation | Ads Live vs real ad delivery; MID → Cust ID linking | Data stays honest | | Fingerprint polling | Onboarding cases, Lead Gen, CSM screens | Fast, near-real-time screens | | Piggyback clock | 5-minute lead sync runs all timed jobs | No scheduler to maintain | | Feature flags | DND enrolment, win-back go-live | Safe rollout without release | | Throttling caps | Win-back 150/run, DND 2000/run | Spread load |

# Pi Commerce Call Center Disposition — Project Explanation

## What it is

An internal web portal for the Pi Commerce calling teams. It replaced a Google Sheet ("Disposition Sheet - Sellers") where agents logged every call to a merchant by hand.

Now an agent logs in, looks up a merchant by **Cust ID** (or phone), sees that merchant's full call history, and logs the outcome of the new call (the **disposition**). Everything is stored in a Neon Postgres database, and on top of that the portal runs work queues, WhatsApp follow-ups, analytics and incentive payouts.

## The three teams (workspaces)

The portal has three workspaces. What a person can open depends on their access (`lib/workspace-access.ts`, `lib/teams.ts`).

| Workspace | Team | Job | Main screen |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Seller** | Sales (BDE / SBDE / TL) | Sell subscriptions to merchants | `app/page.tsx` → `components/AgentConsole.tsx` |
| **Onboarding** | Onboarding | Get a merchant who just paid to their first live ad | `app/onboarding` → `components/OnboardingConsole.tsx` |
| **CSM** | Customer Success | Merchants whose ads have run: renewals, top-ups, upgrades | `app/csm` → `components/CsmConsole.tsx` |

The customer moves through them in order: **Seller sells → Onboarding gets the ad live → CSM keeps the merchant paying.**

## Core idea: dispositions

Each call is logged with a three-level outcome:

- **L0**: the broad result, e.g. Interested, Not Connected, Callback, Not Interested, Plan Upgraded
- **L1**: a sub-reason
- **L2**: the specific detail

The tree lives in database tables (`disposition_nodes`, `onboarding_disposition_nodes`), so admins can change it without a code deploy.

Data-safety rules:

- **Every call creates a new row.** Old calls are never edited, and same-day calls are never merged.
- **The label text is copied onto the call when it's saved.** Renaming a disposition later doesn't rewrite history.
- **Historical calls from the old Google Sheet are kept exactly as they were** (old status and remark text). They are never forced into L0/L1/L2.

## Main features

### Seller workspace
- Search a customer, see their timeline, log a call.
- Book callbacks (`/api/callbacks/my`) and add leads for people not yet in the merchant list (`external_leads`).
- **Lead Gen**: Meta ad-form leads come in from a Google Sheet every 5 minutes and are shared round robin among the sellers switched on for it (`lib/leadgen.ts`).
- Pick a plan on a sale. Plans start 1 Oct 2026; before that every sale was the ₹799 plan (`lib/plans.ts`).

### Onboarding workspace
- A sale creates an **onboarding case**, given automatically to the next person on the onboarding roster (`lib/onboarding.ts`).
- The case tracks subscription data from "Sub Raw" (plan, credits, expiry, stage).
- **Daily backlog rebalance at 8:30 AM IST**: untouched cases move from the live team to the backlog team, max 10 each. Cases tagged Language Barrier are never moved (`lib/onboarding-rebalance.ts`).
- Cases from on-ground Merchant Lending sellers are highlighted in yellow.

### CSM workspace
- Built from the daily **SMB Daily Tracker** sync (Sub Raw + AdsRun Raw).
- Each merchant whose ads have run lands in one queue: `ending`, `ended`, `cancelled`, `lapsed`, `onb_lost`, or `closed` (`lib/csm.ts`).
- CSMs log outcomes such as Top-up, Plan Upgraded, Renewed or Refund requested.

### WhatsApp nudges (`lib/wa.ts`)
- Sent automatically after a "Not Connected" call, and to CSM queues after each daily sync (templates T1–T5).
- Every message has a unique **"Request a callback"** link (`/cb/<token>`, `app/cb/[token]`). A click shows up in the team's *Req Call Back* pane.
- Merchants marked Not Interested / Refund get no messages.

### Payments (CleverTap)
- The CleverTap `payment_success` webhook posts to `/api/internal/ct-payment`. Each sale is stored with the employee code of whoever brought it in (`ct_payment_events`).
- Payments that arrive with only a MID are linked to a Cust ID later (`lib/ct.ts`).

### Analytics & incentives
- `app/analytics`: Seller Analytics, Onboarding Analytics, and the Incentives tab.
- Counts total attempts vs unique customers, fresh vs repeat customers, and connect rate (`lib/status.ts`, `lib/analytics-classification.ts`).
- **Incentives** (`lib/incentives.ts`): seller daily/weekly/revenue plans, onboarder case and top-up pay, TL share, renewal pay. All rules are **date-effective**: a new rule is added with a start date and old rules are never edited, so days already paid don't change.
- Excel payout workbook download (`lib/incentive-workbook.ts`, uses `exceljs`). A finance-only "Incentives" access shows just this tab.

### Admin
- `app/admin/agents`: create and manage people.
- `app/admin/access`: workspace access, teams (with an effective date), seller roles (BDE/SBDE/TL), rosters. Changes are recorded in `access_audit_log`.

## How data gets in

Google Sheets stay the source of truth for merchant data. **Google Apps Script** files push the data into the portal on a timer:

| Script | Pushes | To endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| `docs/google-sheets-merchant-sync.gs` | Merchant list (~40k merchants) | `/api/admin/merchant-sync` |
| `scripts/csm-sync.gs` | Sub Raw + AdsRun Raw (daily) | `/api/internal/csm-sync` |
| `scripts/sub-raw-onboarding-sync.gs` | Sub Raw → onboarding cases | `/api/internal/sub-raw-onboarding-sync` |
| `scripts/leadgen-sync.gs` | Meta lead-form leads (every 5 min) | `/api/internal/leadgen-sync` |
| `scripts/ad-conversions-sync.gs` | Conversions per ad | `/api/internal/ad-conversions-sync` |

These endpoints are protected with shared secrets (`MERCHANT_SYNC_SECRET`, `SUB_RAW_SYNC_SECRET`, `CT_WEBHOOK_SECRET`).

Once-a-day jobs (like the rebalance) are claimed in the `daily_jobs` table so they never run twice on the same day.

## Tech stack

- **Next.js 15** (App Router) + **React 19** + TypeScript, hosted on **Vercel**
- **Neon Postgres**, accessed with the `postgres` library through `lib/db.ts` (pooled connection, no prepared statements so it works with Neon's pooler)
- No ORM. SQL is written directly in the API routes and in `lib/`.
- Login: username + password (`lib/password.ts`), sessions stored in a `sessions` table (`lib/auth.ts`)
- `exceljs` for reading the old workbook and building payout files

## Folder map

```
app/            Pages and API routes (app/api/**/route.ts)
  api/internal/ Endpoints for Apps Script syncs and webhooks (secret-protected)
components/     The big client consoles (Seller, Onboarding, CSM, Lead Gen, Teams…)
lib/            Business logic: auth, plans, incentives, WhatsApp, rosters, CSM queues
db/             SQL migrations 001–032, run in order. Additive only; existing data is never changed.
scripts/        CLI scripts (DB setup, seeding, one-time migration, create agent) + Apps Script files
migration/      Encrypted historical payload from the old sheet
source/         Original prototype HTML
docs/           Merchant sync Apps Script, source baseline counts
.github/        Workflow that runs the Neon migration
```

## Database at a glance

Main tables (full list in `db/*.sql`):

- `customers`, `calls`: merchants and every interaction with them (seller calls)
- `agents`, `sessions`, `workspace_access`, `team_changes`, `seller_roles`: people and access
- `disposition_nodes`, `onboarding_disposition_nodes`: the L0/L1/L2 trees
- `onboarding_cases`, `onboarding_events`, `onboarding_roster`: onboarding
- `merchant_information`, `merchant_subscriptions`, `merchant_ads`, `csm_*`: synced merchant data and CSM
- `leadgen_leads`, `leadgen_roster`: Lead Gen
- `wa_messages`: WhatsApp sends and callback clicks
- `ct_payment_events`: CleverTap payments
- `daily_jobs`: once-a-day job lock

## Running locally

1. `npm install`
2. Create `.env.local` (copy `.env.example`):
   - `DATABASE_URL`: Neon pooled connection string (Neon console → project → **Connect**)
   - `SESSION_SECRET`: any long random string (`openssl rand -base64 32`)
   - `DIRECT_URL`: optional, the non-pooled string for scripts
   - Optional for WhatsApp/sync testing: `PI_WA_*`, `CT_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `MERCHANT_SYNC_SECRET`, `SUB_RAW_SYNC_SECRET` (get them with `vercel link` then `vercel env pull`)
3. `npm run dev` → http://localhost:3000

Useful scripts:

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `npm run db:setup` | Run SQL migrations |
| `npm run db:seed` | Load the disposition tree |
| `npm run agent:create -- --username x --name "X" --password "..." --role admin` | Create a login |
| `npm run source:report` / `migrate:data` / `migrate:validate` | One-time import from the old sheet, and the check that counts match |
| `npm run test:incentives` | Check the incentive math |

Note: `.env.local` is in `.gitignore`. Never put real secrets in `.env.example`.

## Repo

https://github.com/MRG15/Pi-Commerce-Call-Center-Disposition-

66	- `app/analytics`: Seller Analytics, Onboarding Analytics, and the Incentives tab.
67	- Counts total attempts vs unique customers, fresh vs repeat customers, and connect rate (`lib/status.ts`, `lib/analytics-classification.ts`).
68	- **Incentives** (`lib/incentives.ts`): seller daily/weekly/revenue plans, onboarder case and top-up pay, TL share, renewal pay. All rules are **date-effective**: a new rule is added with a start date and old rules are never edited, so days already paid don't change.
69	- Excel payout workbook download (`lib/incentive-workbook.ts`, uses `exceljs`). A finance-only "Incentives" access shows just this tab.
70	
71	### Admin
72	- `app/admin/agents`: create and manage people.
73	- `app/admin/access`: workspace access, teams (with an effective date), seller roles (BDE/SBDE/TL), rosters. Changes are recorded in `access_audit_log`.
74	
75	## How data gets in
76	
77	Google Sheets stay the source of truth for merchant data. **Google Apps Script** files push the data into the portal on a timer:
78	
79	| Script | Pushes | To endpoint |
80	|---|---|---|
81	| `docs/google-sheets-merchant-sync.gs` | Merchant list (~40k merchants) | `/api/admin/merchant-sync` |
82	| `scripts/csm-sync.gs` | Sub Raw + AdsRun Raw (daily) | `/api/internal/csm-sync` |
83	| `scripts/sub-raw-onboarding-sync.gs` | Sub Raw → onboarding cases | `/api/internal/sub-raw-onboarding-sync` |
84	| `scripts/leadgen-sync.gs` | Meta lead-form leads (every 5 min) | `/api/internal/leadgen-sync` |
85	| `scripts/ad-conversions-sync.gs` | Conversions per ad | `/api/internal/ad-conversions-sync` |
86	
87	These endpoints are protected with shared secrets (`MERCHANT_SYNC_SECRET`, `SUB_RAW_SYNC_SECRET`, `CT_WEBHOOK_SECRET`).
88	
89	Once-a-day jobs (like the rebalance) are claimed in the `daily_jobs` table so they never run twice on the same day.
90	
91	## Tech stack
92	
93	- **Next.js 15** (App Router) + **React 19** + TypeScript, hosted on **Vercel**
94	- **Neon Postgres**, accessed with the `postgres` library through `lib/db.ts` (pooled connection, no prepared statements so it works with Neon's pooler)
95	- No ORM. SQL is written directly in the API routes and in `lib/`.
96	- Login: username + password (`lib/password.ts`), sessions stored in a `sessions` table (`lib/auth.ts`)
97	- `exceljs` for reading the old workbook and building payout files
98	
99	## Folder map
100	
101	```
102	app/            Pages and API routes (app/api/**/route.ts)
103	  api/internal/ Endpoints for Apps Script syncs and webhooks (secret-protected)
104	components/     The big client consoles (Seller, Onboarding, CSM, Lead Gen, Teams…)
105	lib/            Business logic: auth, plans, incentives, WhatsApp, rosters, CSM queues
106	db/             SQL migrations 001–032, run in order. Additive only; existing data is never changed.
107	scripts/        CLI scripts (DB setup, seeding, one-time migration, create agent) + Apps Script files
108	migration/      Encrypted historical payload from the old sheet
109	source/         Original prototype HTML
110	docs/           Merchant sync Apps Script, source baseline counts
111	.github/        Workflow that runs the Neon migration
112	```
113	
114	## Database at a glance
115	
116	Main tables (full list in `db/*.sql`):
117	
118	- `customers`, `calls`: merchants and every interaction with them (seller calls)
119	- `agents`, `sessions`, `workspace_access`, `team_changes`, `seller_roles`: people and access
120	- `disposition_nodes`, `onboarding_disposition_nodes`: the L0/L1/L2 trees
121	- `onboarding_cases`, `onboarding_events`, `onboarding_roster`: onboarding
122	- `merchant_information`, `merchant_subscriptions`, `merchant_ads`, `csm_*`: synced merchant data and CSM
123	- `leadgen_leads`, `leadgen_roster`: Lead Gen
124	- `wa_messages`: WhatsApp sends and callback clicks
125	- `ct_payment_events`: CleverTap payments
126	- `daily_jobs`: once-a-day job lock
127	
128	## Running locally
129	
130	1. `npm install`
131	2. Create `.env.local` (copy `.env.example`):
132	   - `DATABASE_URL`: Neon pooled connection string (Neon console → project → **Connect**)
133	   - `SESSION_SECRET`: any long random string (`openssl rand -base64 32`)
134	   - `DIRECT_URL`: optional, the non-pooled string for scripts
135	   - Optional for WhatsApp/sync testing: `PI_WA_*`, `CT_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, `MERCHANT_SYNC_SECRET`, `SUB_RAW_SYNC_SECRET` (get them with `vercel link` then `vercel env pull`)
136	3. `npm run dev` → http://localhost:3000
137	
138	Useful scripts:
139	
140	| Command | Does |
141	|---|---|
142	| `npm run db:setup` | Run SQL migrations |
143	| `npm run db:seed` | Load the disposition tree |
144	| `npm run agent:create -- --username x --name "X" --password "..." --role admin` | Create a login |
145	| `npm run source:report` / `migrate:data` / `migrate:validate` | One-time import from the old sheet, and the check that counts match |
146	| `npm run test:incentives` | Check the incentive math |
147	
148	Note: `.env.local` is in `.gitignore`. Never put real secrets in `.env.example`.
149	
150	## Repo
151	
152	https://github.com/MRG15/Pi-Commerce-Call-Center-Disposition-
153

# PDF Processing Guide

## Overview

This guide covers essential PDF processing operations using Python libraries and command-line tools. For advanced features, JavaScript libraries, and detailed examples, see REFERENCE.md. If you need to fill out a PDF form, read FORMS.md and follow its instructions.

## Quick Start

```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Read a PDF
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
print(f"Pages: {len(reader.pages)}")

# Extract text
text = ""
for page in reader.pages:
    text += page.extract_text()
```

## Python Libraries

### pypdf - Basic Operations

#### Merge PDFs
```python
from pypdf import PdfWriter, PdfReader

writer = PdfWriter()
for pdf_file in ["doc1.pdf", "doc2.pdf", "doc3.pdf"]:
    reader = PdfReader(pdf_file)
    for page in reader.pages:
        writer.add_page(page)

with open("merged.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

#### Split PDF
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
for i, page in enumerate(reader.pages):
    writer = PdfWriter()
    writer.add_page(page)
    with open(f"page_{i+1}.pdf", "wb") as output:
        writer.write(output)
```

#### Extract Metadata
```python
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
meta = reader.metadata
print(f"Title: {meta.title}")
print(f"Author: {meta.author}")
print(f"Subject: {meta.subject}")
print(f"Creator: {meta.creator}")
```

#### Rotate Pages
```python
reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

page = reader.pages[0]
page.rotate(90)  # Rotate 90 degrees clockwise
writer.add_page(page)

with open("rotated.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### pdfplumber - Text and Table Extraction

#### Extract Text with Layout
```python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for page in pdf.pages:
        text = page.extract_text()
        print(text)
```

#### Extract Tables
```python
with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    for i, page in enumerate(pdf.pages):
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for j, table in enumerate(tables):
            print(f"Table {j+1} on page {i+1}:")
            for row in table:
                print(row)
```

#### Advanced Table Extraction
```python
import pandas as pd

with pdfplumber.open("document.pdf") as pdf:
    all_tables = []
    for page in pdf.pages:
        tables = page.extract_tables()
        for table in tables:
            if table:  # Check if table is not empty
                df = pd.DataFrame(table[1:], columns=table[0])
                all_tables.append(df)

# Combine all tables
if all_tables:
    combined_df = pd.concat(all_tables, ignore_index=True)
    combined_df.to_excel("extracted_tables.xlsx", index=False)
```

### reportlab - Create PDFs

#### Basic PDF Creation
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.pdfgen import canvas

c = canvas.Canvas("hello.pdf", pagesize=letter)
width, height = letter

# Add text
c.drawString(100, height - 100, "Hello World!")
c.drawString(100, height - 120, "This is a PDF created with reportlab")

# Add a line
c.line(100, height - 140, 400, height - 140)

# Save
c.save()
```

#### Create PDF with Multiple Pages
```python
from reportlab.lib.pagesizes import letter
from reportlab.platypus import SimpleDocTemplate, Paragraph, Spacer, PageBreak
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

doc = SimpleDocTemplate("report.pdf", pagesize=letter)
styles = getSampleStyleSheet()
story = []

# Add content
title = Paragraph("Report Title", styles['Title'])
story.append(title)
story.append(Spacer(1, 12))

body = Paragraph("This is the body of the report. " * 20, styles['Normal'])
story.append(body)
story.append(PageBreak())

# Page 2
story.append(Paragraph("Page 2", styles['Heading1']))
story.append(Paragraph("Content for page 2", styles['Normal']))

# Build PDF
doc.build(story)
```

#### Subscripts and Superscripts

**IMPORTANT**: Never use Unicode subscript/superscript characters (₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉, ⁰¹²³⁴⁵⁶⁷⁸⁹) in ReportLab PDFs. The built-in fonts do not include these glyphs, causing them to render as solid black boxes.

Instead, use ReportLab's XML markup tags in Paragraph objects:
```python
from reportlab.platypus import Paragraph
from reportlab.lib.styles import getSampleStyleSheet

styles = getSampleStyleSheet()

# Subscripts: use <sub> tag
chemical = Paragraph("H<sub>2</sub>O", styles['Normal'])

# Superscripts: use <super> tag
squared = Paragraph("x<super>2</super> + y<super>2</super>", styles['Normal'])
```

For canvas-drawn text (not Paragraph objects), manually adjust font the size and position rather than using Unicode subscripts/superscripts.

## Command-Line Tools

### pdftotext (poppler-utils)
```bash
# Extract text
pdftotext input.pdf output.txt

# Extract text preserving layout
pdftotext -layout input.pdf output.txt

# Extract specific pages
pdftotext -f 1 -l 5 input.pdf output.txt  # Pages 1-5
```

### qpdf
```bash
# Merge PDFs
qpdf --empty --pages file1.pdf file2.pdf -- merged.pdf

# Split pages
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 1-5 -- pages1-5.pdf
qpdf input.pdf --pages . 6-10 -- pages6-10.pdf

# Rotate pages
qpdf input.pdf output.pdf --rotate=+90:1  # Rotate page 1 by 90 degrees

# Remove password
qpdf --[redacted] --decrypt encrypted.pdf decrypted.pdf
```

### pdftk (if available)
```bash
# Merge
pdftk file1.pdf file2.pdf cat output merged.pdf

# Split
pdftk input.pdf burst

# Rotate
pdftk input.pdf rotate 1east output rotated.pdf
```

## Common Tasks

### Extract Text from Scanned PDFs
```python
# Requires: pip install pytesseract pdf2image
import pytesseract
from pdf2image import convert_from_path

# Convert PDF to images
images = convert_from_path('scanned.pdf')

# OCR each page
text = ""
for i, image in enumerate(images):
    text += f"Page {i+1}:\n"
    text += pytesseract.image_to_string(image)
    text += "\n\n"

print(text)
```

### Add Watermark
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

# Create watermark (or load existing)
watermark = PdfReader("watermark.pdf").pages[0]

# Apply to all pages
reader = PdfReader("document.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    page.merge_page(watermark)
    writer.add_page(page)

with open("watermarked.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

### Extract Images
```bash
# Using pdfimages (poppler-utils)
pdfimages -j input.pdf output_prefix

# This extracts all images as output_prefix-000.jpg, output_prefix-001.jpg, etc.
```

### Password Protection
```python
from pypdf import PdfReader, PdfWriter

reader = PdfReader("input.pdf")
writer = PdfWriter()

for page in reader.pages:
    writer.add_page(page)

# Add password
writer.encrypt("userpassword", "ownerpassword")

with open("encrypted.pdf", "wb") as output:
    writer.write(output)
```

## Quick Reference

| Task | Best Tool | Command/Code |
|------|-----------|--------------|
| Merge PDFs | pypdf | `writer.add_page(page)` |
| Split PDFs | pypdf | One page per file |
| Extract text | pdfplumber | `page.extract_text()` |
| Extract tables | pdfplumber | `page.extract_tables()` |
| Create PDFs | reportlab | Canvas or Platypus |
| Command line merge | qpdf | `qpdf --empty --pages ...` |
| OCR scanned PDFs | pytesseract | Convert to image first |
| Fill PDF forms | pdf-lib or pypdf (see FORMS.md) | See FORMS.md |

## Next Steps

- For advanced pypdfium2 usage, see REFERENCE.md
- For JavaScript libraries (pdf-lib), see REFERENCE.md
- If you need to fill out a PDF form, follow the instructions in FORMS.md
- For troubleshooting guides, see REFERENCE.md

(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

- footprint: Local SLM that learns from Claude Code transcripts ("footprint") and replays the project's working style. Trigger on /footprint, "take footprint", "train footprint", "footprint status", "footprint run <task>".
- keploy-api-tests: No-MCP, log-driven Keploy record/replay loop, driven by `keploy status` NEXT blocks.
- vercel:bootstrap: Bootstrap a repository with Vercel-linked resources by running preflight checks, provisioning integrations, verifying env keys, and then executing db/dev startup commands safely.
- vercel:deploy: Deploy the current project to Vercel. Pass "prod" or "production" as argument to deploy to production. Default is preview deployment.
- vercel:env: Manage Vercel environment variables. Commands include list, pull, add, remove, and diff. Use to sync environment variables between Vercel and your local development environment.
- vercel:status: Show the status of the current Vercel project — recent deployments, linked project info, and environment overview.
- pdf-viewer:annotate: Collaboratively annotate a PDF — propose markup, review together, iterate
- pdf-viewer:fill-form: Fill PDF form fields interactively with live visual feedback
- pdf-viewer:open: Open a PDF in the interactive viewer
- pdf-viewer:sign: Place a signature or initials image on a PDF
- caveman:caveman: Ultra-compressed communication mode. Cuts token usage ~75% by speaking like caveman while keeping full technical accuracy. Supports intensity levels: lite, full (default), ultra, wenyan-lite, wenyan-full, wenyan-ultra. Use when user says "caveman mode", "talk like caveman", "use caveman", "less tokens", "be brief", or invokes /caveman. Also auto-triggers when token efficiency is requested.
- caveman:caveman-commit: Ultra-compressed commit message generator. Cuts noise from commit messages while preserving intent and reasoning. Conventional Commits format. Subject ≤50 chars, body only when "why" isn't obvious. Use when user says "write a commit", "commit message", "generate commit", "/commit", or invokes /caveman-commit. Auto-triggers when staging changes.
- caveman:caveman-help: Quick-reference card for all caveman modes, skills, and commands. One-shot display, not a persistent mode. Trigger: /caveman-help, "caveman help", "what caveman commands", "how do I use caveman".
- caveman:caveman-review: Ultra-compressed code review comments. Cuts noise from PR feedback while preserving the actionable signal. Each comment is one line: location, problem, fix. Use when user says "review this PR", "code review", "review the diff", "/review", or invokes /caveman-review. Auto-triggers when reviewing pull requests.
- caveman:compress: Compress natural language memory files (CLAUDE.md, todos, preferences) into caveman format to save input tokens. Preserves all technical substance, code, URLs, and structure. Compressed version overwrites the original file. Human-readable backup saved as FILE.original.md. Trigger: /caveman:compress <filepath> or "compress memory file"
- vercel:access-protected-vercel-deployment: Access and test Vercel deployments protected by Vercel Authentication, SSO, or Deployment Protection. Use when curl, agent-browser, Playwright, or another automated request reaches a Vercel login or protection page; when a protected preview or production URL returns 401 or 403; when TRUSTED_SOURCES_ENVIRONMENT_MISMATCH appears; or when choosing between `vercel curl` and the `x-vercel-trusted-oidc-idp-token` header.
- vercel:ai-gateway: Vercel AI Gateway guidance for setup, model discovery, authentication, routing, fallbacks, BYOK, budgets, spend reporting, observability, compatible APIs, and coding-agent configuration. Use when adding AI Gateway to an app, migrating provider calls, choosing models or providers, debugging gateway requests, or running `vercel ai-gateway` commands.
- vercel:ai-sdk: Vercel AI SDK expert guidance. Use when building AI-powered features — chat interfaces, text generation, structured output, tool calling, agents, MCP integration, streaming, embeddings, reranking, image generation, or working with any LLM provider.
- vercel:auth: Authentication integration guidance — Clerk (native Vercel Marketplace), Descope, and Auth0 setup for Next.js applications, plus Sign in with Vercel, Vercel Passport, and Vercel KMS. Covers proxy.ts auth patterns, sign-in/sign-up flows, and Marketplace provisioning. Use when implementing user authentication or protecting deployments.
- vercel:build-agents: Default guidance for building AI agents. Use for generic requests to build, create, scaffold, design, architect, or implement an AI agent, agent app, tool-calling agent, durable agent, multi-agent system, or scheduled agent.
- vercel:cdn-caching: Debug Vercel CDN caching — cache hit rate, stale content, revalidation behavior, ISR + PPR, per-request cache reasons (cacheReason) and PPR state (ppr_state), and costs.
- vercel:chat-sdk: Vercel Chat SDK expert guidance. Use when building multi-platform chat bots — Slack, Telegram, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Google Chat, GitHub, Linear — with a single codebase. Covers the Chat class, adapters, threads, messages, cards, modals, streaming, state management, and webhook setup.
- vercel:create-a-backend: Backend architecture guidance. Use when planning, building, or migrating an API or backend; choosing between Functions, Services, containers, Workflow, Queues, and Marketplace databases; or selecting a supported backend framework or runtime.
- vercel:custom-metrics: Emit and query Vercel Custom Metrics. Use when instrumenting application or business measurements in Vercel Functions, using metric() from @vercel/functions, choosing metric names and attributes, or querying emitted values with vc metrics.
- vercel:deployments-cicd: Vercel deployment and CI/CD expert guidance. Use when deploying, promoting, rolling back, inspecting deployments, building with --prebuilt, or configuring CI workflow files for Vercel.
- vercel:env-vars: Vercel environment variable expert guidance. Use when working with .env files, vercel env commands, OIDC tokens, or managing environment-specific configuration.
- vercel:eve: eve framework guidance for durable AI agents and agent-powered applications. Use when creating, editing, or debugging an eve project, when the user explicitly asks for eve, or when the build-agents skill has selected eve as the default framework. Covers eve's filesystem-first runtime, durable sessions, tools, skills, connections, channels, sandboxes, subagents, schedules, evals, frontend clients, and Agent Runs observability. ## claude.ai Figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

FILE SESSION:
Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session with that key and a concise task description before search_design_system, get_libraries, use_figma, or any other file tool. This applies to read-only tasks too. If a new file is needed, call create_new_file first, then create_session with the returned file key. Reuse the returned UUID as the sessionId argument on eligible file tools for subsequent work on that task, including calls to other files.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
</system-reminder>
